sources.title: Educational attainment
sources.measures: Why the federal labor statistics agency reports educational attainment for adults starting at the age by which most people have finished schooling.
sources.excerpt: Educational attainment data published by BLS typically pertain to people age 25 and older because most people have completed their schooling by age 25.

milestones.label: The end of formal schooling for most people
milestones.population: Adults in the Current Population Survey; the federal labor statistics agency reports attainment from this age because most people have finished schooling by then.
whatChanges: National attainment tables begin counting at the age where most people have stopped adding formal credentials, which is why the young adult bands are reported separately.
Schooling that continues past that point still happens, and it appears in later attainment figures rather than in the young adult ones.

milestones.label: Finishing a bachelor's degree
milestones.population: Bachelor's degree recipients in a national follow-up study of graduates, grouped by the age at which they completed degree requirements; the oldest group in that table is open ended, so the upper edge here is where that group starts rather than where it ends.
whatChanges: The rest of the graduating group finishes later, some in the second half of the twenties and some at thirty or beyond.
The stretch between first enrolling and the degree runs much longer for recipients who finish at older ages, so the calendar and the credential come apart.
This counts only people who reached the degree; it says nothing about how many started.

milestones.label: Living in a parent's home as a young adult
milestones.population: Adults in the younger of the Current Population Survey young adult age bands, where living in a parent's home was the most common arrangement; these are the survey's reporting bands rather than the outer edges of the arrangement.
whatChanges: Students living in college housing are recorded at a parent's address in this survey, so the count mixes staying home with being away at school.
In the late teens and early twenties it is the most common arrangement the survey records; in the older young adult band it is a minority one, and it stays far from rare.
The bands are the survey's own brackets, so they mark where the counting is grouped rather than where the arrangement begins or ends.

milestones.label: Leaving a parent's home
milestones.population: United States respondents born in the early nineteen-eighties and followed by a national longitudinal survey of youth; the lower edge is where the study reports most departures completed and the upper edge is where nearly all of them had left.
whatChanges: The decline runs steeper in the United States than in the comparison countries in the same study, and nearly all departures had happened by thirty.
The measurement follows one cohort born in the early nineteen-eighties, so it describes their passage rather than a rule about anyone now.
Housing costs and study both move this timing, which is why the same event lands at different ages in different countries.

milestones.label: Learning that continues after formal schooling ends
milestones.researchNote: No age-resolved United States figure was obtainable. The adult skills assessment pages fetched report fixed survey universes only (working-age adults, plus an older extension band) and no measured age at which adult learning begins, peaks, or ends, so any window would be the survey universe dressed up as an age. Resolving query: NCES Program for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies United States results tables giving literacy proficiency by ten-year age group, or the NCES Adult Training and Education Survey reporting participation in work-related courses and certificate programs by age group.
milestones.windowInWords: Formal and informal learning continues after schooling ends and across adult life, but no sourced age window for it was found.
